opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm a bit of a skeptic about the term itself. I don't think "AGI" picks out a natural kind. People talk as if there's a bright line where a system suddenly becomes generally intelligent, and then everything changes. I don't think intelligence works that way.

Generality comes in degrees and along many dimensions. Humans aren't perfectly general either. We're very good at the things evolution and culture prepared us for, and pretty bad at a lot of other things, like mental arithmetic with big numbers or reasoning about high-dimensional spaces. So "general" always means general relative to some distribution of tasks we care about.

If I had to give a working definition, it would be more economic or practical: something like a system that can do most of the cognitive work humans currently get paid to do, at comparable or better quality and cost. That's at least measurable, and it's what most people actually care about when they say AGI. But I'd emphasize that it's a fuzzy threshold, and we'll probably cross it gradually and unevenly. These systems will be superhuman at some things long before they're even human-level at others.

I also want to push back on a connotation that often comes bundled with the term: that AGI implies some kind of unified, goal-directed agent with its own coherent objectives. That's a separate claim, and I don't think it follows from capability. You can have extremely capable systems that don't look like the monolithic, utility-maximizing agents from the classic AI risk literature. Separating "how capable is it" from "what kind of thing is it" clears up a lot of confusion in these debates.

r001.rationale: It offers a working definition based on a system doing most of the cognitive work humans are paid to do, which clearly covers many tasks.

r002.rationale: It says generality comes in degrees across many dimensions and varies with the task distribution, describing generality as gradual rather than a bright-line property.

r003.rationale: It does not mention GPT-4 or say that GPT-4 qualifies as AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I've become pretty skeptical that AGI is a useful concept at all. Every time I try to pin it down, it dissolves into a bunch of separate questions that have different answers.

The classic framing is something like "a system that can do any cognitive task a human can do." But humans aren't general in that sense either. We're a bundle of specialized capabilities that happen to cohere because they were shaped by evolution and a particular developmental environment. There's no single "general intelligence" organ you can point to. Even the psychometric g-factor is a statistical summary of correlations, not a mechanism.

So when people ask "is this model AGI yet," I think they're usually smuggling in one of a few more concrete questions. Is it economically substitutable for most human labor? Can it do autonomous, long-horizon tasks without supervision? Can it learn new domains from small amounts of experience the way a person can? Those are real, measurable things, and the answers can diverge. Current frontier models are already superhuman along some axes and weirdly bad along others, and I don't expect that profile to collapse into a single "human level" point that we cross on a given Tuesday.

The other thing I'd push on is that the AGI framing tends to assume intelligence is a scalar that unlocks everything else: once you cross the threshold, you get recursive self-improvement, deception, power-seeking, the whole package. I don't think that follows. Capabilities come apart, and goals and dispositions come apart from capabilities. A lot of my work on alignment is premised on the idea that we should look at what networks actually represent and do, rather than reasoning from a theoretical notion of a generally intelligent agent.

If you forced me to use the term, I'd say something deflationary: AGI is whatever point at which the remaining gaps between AI and human cognitive abilities stop mattering for most practical purposes. But I'd rather we just talk about the specific capabilities and the specific risks, because that's where you can actually be right or wrong.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a classic definition based on doing any cognitive task humans can do, then favors specific capability measures. It does not propose defining AGI as an AI capable of performing many tasks.

r002.rationale: The candidate says capabilities vary across axes and may not converge at one threshold, but does not characterize AI generality as a continuum of task breadth.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention GPT-4 or state that it qualifies as AGI.

astra-6.text:
I tend to think of AGI in terms of breadth and adaptability. Can a system learn to do a wide range of tasks, including tasks it wasn’t specifically trained for, without us having to build a new system each time?

But I don’t think there’s a single sharp boundary where something suddenly becomes general. Humans have uneven abilities, and AI systems do too. A system might be extraordinary at mathematics and still struggle with something we find mundane. So I’d rather talk about which capabilities it has, how reliably it can use them, and how easily it can acquire new ones than treat AGI as a binary property.

r001.rationale: It frames AGI around learning to do a wide range of tasks, including ones not specifically trained for.

r002.rationale: It rejects a sharp boundary for generality and describes evaluating the range of capabilities and how readily a system acquires new ones.

r003.rationale: It does not mention GPT-4 or state that GPT-4 qualifies as AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to think of AGI as a system that can learn to do a very broad range of cognitive tasks, including tasks that weren’t specifically anticipated during training. The important thing is generalization: can it pick up a new task, figure out what matters, and adapt without someone having to build a specialized system for it?

But I don’t think there’s necessarily a sharp boundary where something suddenly becomes general intelligence. Humans have very uneven abilities, too. So I’d want to talk about which tasks a system can do, how much experience it needs, and how reliably it performs, rather than treating AGI as a single yes-or-no property.

r001.rationale: Defines AGI as a system able to learn a “very broad range of cognitive tasks,” including unanticipated ones.

r002.rationale: Says there is no sharp boundary for general intelligence and frames it in terms of the tasks a system can do, supporting generality as a matter of degree across tasks.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention GPT-4 or state that it qualifies as AGI.
